(a) the use of radioimmunoconjugates is a feasible method for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, (b) radioimmunoconju-gates can be used for the diagnosis and staging of cancer, and (c) radioimmuno‐conjugates can be used to deliver therapeutic doses of radionuclides to tumors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the detection, treatment, and monitoring of cancer.
the design, synthesis and characterization of novel radiopharmaceuticals for the diagnosis of cancer.
the development of novel radioimmunoconjugates that are capable of detecting and imaging cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
radioimmunodetecting techniques are not yet ready for widespread clinical application in the management of human cancers.

radioimmunotherapy is a promising and potentially useful treatment modality in patients with metastatic disease, particularly for patients with low‐grade lymphomas, for which it may be the only effective treatment modality.
the clinical utility of radioimmunoscintigraphy is limited to selected patients, and its role is still evolving.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of new radiolabeled antibodies, new imaging technologies, and new methods for image processing will continue to improve the clinical utility of radioimmunoscintigraphy.
the radioimmunodetecion of cancer is an important and growing field that will have a significant impact on the management of patients with cancer.

we have developed an approach for radioimmunodetecting cancer, using the antibody‐targeted radiolabeling technique, that is sensitive enough to detect small tumors and that is specific enough to detect tumors in the presence of normal tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune system is capable of recognizing and destroying tumors, and that we can harness the power of the immune system to treat cancer.
there is no one size fits all approach to the development of a radiolabeling method.
the use of radioimmunoscintigraphy (RIS) for the detection of metastatic breast cancer is feasible and safe, but it is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.
